paragraphs: Luton Borough Council runs its own fostering service, and the independent agencies shown above also approve carers in the town. Fostering for the council means caring for Luton's own children, with the council's social workers supporting you; an independent agency carries out your assessment, approves and supervises you itself, and looks after children placed with it by councils.

In March 2025 the council said it looks after over 300 children and young people, and that many of them live outside Luton because the town does not have enough fostering families. Its sufficiency strategy for 2025 to 2030 makes recruiting and keeping its own carers the first priority. It records that 26.2% of placements in March 2025 were more than 20 miles away and aims to bring that under 18% within three years, plans 24 new council fostering households between April 2025 and March 2027, and wants to rely less on agencies. It also wants its carers to reflect Luton's cultural, ethnic and faith diversity, and is working with churches, mosques, temples and cultural associations to reach more people.

The council pays a weekly allowance for each child, from £189 for babies to £288 for 16 and 17-year-olds, and a weekly skills fee per child that rises with experience, from £145.90 in a carer's first year with Luton to £259.13 after five years. Birthday, festive and holiday allowances are paid on top, along with a £1,000 contribution towards Council Tax. Our Luton allowance page has the full scale.

Getting started takes around six months, sometimes longer. You register interest through Foster East, the service Luton shares with Central Bedfordshire and Bedford Borough, and the council says it will be in touch within 24 hours. An information event and a home visit come next, then checks and references, then an assessment of usually around 16 weeks, during which you complete Skills to Foster: six weekly sessions of three hours. A fostering panel then makes its recommendation. With government backing, the three councils are building a shared fostering hub that aims to raise foster capacity across their areas to 478 places by 2028/29.

Once approved, each Luton carer has a supervising social worker and joins the Luton Foster Carers Association. Carers are encouraged to complete at least six training activities in their first 12 months and three a year after that, and the 2026-27 programme runs in person and online, from first aid to diplomas. Luton launched Mockingbird in August 2025, and its first group has nine carers and ten children. Speak to the council and two or three of the agencies above; the Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire and Milton Keynes pages list more services nearby.
